title: Four senses
hookLine: medieval readers found four layers: literal, allegorical, moral, and where it leads

lines: A CITY, A CHURCH, A SOUL, HEAVEN.
cards: How many meanings can one word hold? Try Jerusalem. To a pilgrim, it's a city on a hill, with walls and a temple.

To a monk named John Cassian, writing for other monks, it could be four things at once: the earthly city, the church, the human soul, and the city of God waiting at the end of everything. One word, four rooms.
For many medieval readers, that wasn't a trick. It was how you read the Bible carefully. Today's word: four senses.

teach.b: The four senses are four layers of meaning in a passage of scripture. The literal: what the words say and what happened. The allegorical: what it shows about Christ and the church.
The moral: what it asks of you, how to live. And the one with the hardest name, the anagogical: where it leads, toward the end of all things and the life to come.

A little Latin rhyme, tradition says, summed it up, roughly: the letter teaches what happened, allegory what to believe, the moral what to do, and the anagogy where you're going. There's a seed of it in the Bible itself.
In Galatians, Paul tells of Abraham's two sons, one by Hagar the bondmaid and one by the freewoman, then says: "Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants."
A family story, read as a story about God's promises. Medieval teachers also kept a rule.
Thomas Aquinas taught that the other senses stand on the literal: you don't float off to heaven until you know what the text actually says. Churches have kept this differently.

teach.h: WHERE IT LEADS: WHERE YOU'RE GOING.
teach.b: Catholic teaching still names the four senses. Orthodox readers draw deeply on the early fathers' spiritual readings.
Reformers such as Luther and Calvin pushed hard for the plain sense, wary of allegories that could make a verse mean anything, while still reading Christ throughout the scriptures.
All of them were asking the same thing: how deep does this go?

how: Catholic teaching names the literal sense and three spiritual senses of scripture; Orthodox preaching often draws on the early fathers' spiritual readings, and Protestant preaching, following the Reformers, stresses the plain sense of the text.

games.q: you're a student in a medieval school, reading the word Jerusalem in a psalm. your teacher asks for the fourth sense: where does it lead?
o: the city in Judea, with walls and a temple.
the human soul, and how to live.
the city of God at the end of all things.
games.why: the fourth sense points to the end: the city of God. the city with walls is the literal sense, and the soul is the moral one.

practice: Take the shepherd who finds one sheep missing, goes after it, and carries it home on his shoulders, glad.

Move through it slowly: see the hillside and the search; then the shepherd as Christ, seeking, as some readers have; then who has gone missing from your circle, and whether you'd go looking; then where it leads, since Jesus ends the story with joy in heaven.
If you pray, stay in whichever layer feels like prayer.

wordCard.voice: Four senses. Literal, allegorical, moral, and where it leads: the medieval way of reading one passage on four floors at once.

orig.note: Greek: usually explained as a leading up; the name of the fourth sense, where a text leads.
